name: Communication Studies
description: An elective course exploring how people create meaning through verbal and nonverbal messages, active listening, intrapersonal and interpersonal communication, small-group collaboration, and formal and informal organizational channels. Students analyze fictional, public, or de-identified cases and produce evidence-based communication models, diagrams, and reports.

modules.title: Communication Process & Models
modules.objectives: Identify the key elements of the communication process; compare and contrast linear, interactive, and transactional models of communication.
modules.readingNote: Communication in the Real World §1.2 — transmission, interaction, and transactional models; participants, messages, channels, feedback, context, and noise.
modules.videoNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.practiceNote: Use the section’s three-model comparison as a guide, then map a teacher-provided fictional dialogue to communicators, message, channel, feedback, noise, and context. Do not use a real conversation or private message.
modules.assignment: Use the supplied fictional conversation scenario or create a brief hypothetical exchange. Draw and label a transactional model identifying communicators, message, channel, feedback, noise, and context; then write a 250-word analysis of how physical or psychological noise changes meaning. Submit: the labeled model and analysis. Include: at least one encoding/decoding decision and one feedback loop. Evaluation: model accuracy (35%), application of noise/context (30%), evidence from the scenario (20%), and clarity (15%). Do not use real names, private messages, or sensitive personal details.

modules.title: Verbal Communication
modules.objectives: Explain how language creates meaning; analyze the impact of word choice, clarity, and language style on effective verbal communication.
modules.readingNote: Communication in the Real World §3.1 — symbols, denotation, connotation, language rules, and how people construct meaning.
modules.videoNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.practiceNote: Complete a teacher-adapted version of the section exercises: identify denotative and connotative meaning in public or fictional messages, then revise vague wording for a named audience. Do not use private messages.
modules.assignment: Collect five ambiguous or misleading verbal messages from publicly available headlines, advertisements, or teacher-provided/de-identified examples. For each, rewrite the message for a named audience and explain in about 50 words what made the original unclear. Submit: a five-row before/after table and a 150-word pattern summary. Include: source or scenario label, denotative/connotative issue, revision, audience, and rationale. Evaluation: accurate diagnosis (30%), clearer revisions (30%), audience reasoning (25%), and source traceability/clarity (15%). Do not use private messages or identify private individuals.

modules.title: Nonverbal Communication
modules.objectives: Identify categories of nonverbal communication; analyze how body language, proxemics, and paralanguage convey meaning alongside verbal messages. Students will analyze model texts, draft or revise written responses, and support claims with textual evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: Communication in the Real World §4.1 — principles, ambiguity, credibility, and the reinforcing, substituting, and contradicting functions of nonverbal communication.
modules.videoNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.video2Note: YouTube — Your Body Language May Shape Who You Are (TED)
modules.practiceNote: Use the section’s functions as a coding guide for a teacher-provided or public silent clip. Record literal cues first, then label possible functions and one alternative interpretation.
modules.assignment: Use a teacher-provided or publicly available short scene and review it once without sound. Submit: an observation log with at least ten nonverbal signals and a 300-word analysis. Include: timestamp, kinesics/facial expression/proxemics or other category, literal observation, interpretation, and one alternative interpretation that prevents overclaiming. Evaluation: accurate observation (30%), concept classification (25%), evidence-based interpretation (30%), and alternative explanation/clarity (15%).

modules.title: Listening & Feedback
modules.objectives: Distinguish between hearing and active listening; apply effective feedback strategies to improve communication outcomes. Students will analyze model texts, draft or revise written responses, and support claims with textual evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: Communication in the Real World §5.1 — listening stages, purposes, types, styles, and the effects of physical and psychological noise.
modules.videoNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.video2Note: YouTube — The Power of Listening | William Ury (relevant listening strategies; title verified).
modules.practiceNote: Use §5.3 listening-competence strategies to annotate a teacher-provided fictional transcript or public interview for paraphrase, open questions, feedback, and barriers to listening.
modules.assignment: Use a teacher-provided fictional transcript or a public interview clip. Mark at least six examples of active-listening behavior, including paraphrase, open questions, minimal encouragers, and feedback. Submit: an annotation table plus a 300-word analysis of what helps or blocks understanding. Include: the speaker cue, listener response, technique label, and a justified improvement. Evaluation: correct technique identification (30%), evidence-based analysis (35%), useful revisions (25%), and clarity (10%). No private conversation or personal disclosure is required.

modules.title: Intrapersonal Communication
modules.objectives: Define intrapersonal communication and explain its role in self-concept, self-esteem, and internal dialogue. Students will analyze model texts, draft or revise written responses, and support claims with textual evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: Communication in the Real World §2.3 — self-concept, reflected appraisal, social comparison, and how self-presentation shapes communication.
modules.videoNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.practiceNote: Apply the perception-checking steps to teacher-provided fictional self-talk vignettes. Explain how an interpretation could shape outward communication; do not submit personal reflection or mental-health information.
modules.assignment: Analyze three fictional self-talk vignettes provided in the module: one supportive, one self-critical, and one neutral. For each, explain how the internal message could affect perception, emotion, and outward communication; then rewrite one message in a realistic, constructive form. Submit: a three-row analysis table and a 250–350 word synthesis. Include: the vignette cue, likely interpretation, communication effect, and one constructive rewrite. Evaluation: accurate intrapersonal concepts (35%), cause-and-effect reasoning (30%), constructive revision (20%), and clarity (15%). Do not submit a personal journal or mental-health information.

modules.title: Interpersonal Communication
modules.objectives: Apply principles of interpersonal communication to build, maintain, and repair relationships; explain disclosure and reciprocity. Students will analyze model texts, draft or revise written responses, and support claims with textual evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: Communication in the Real World §6.4 — self-disclosure, reciprocity, social penetration, the Johari Window, and ethical disclosure boundaries.
modules.videoNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.video2Note: YouTube — Think Fast, Talk Smart: Communication Techniques (conversation preparation and responsive speaking; title verified).
modules.practiceNote: Use the section’s Johari Window framework only with teacher-provided fictional characters and observable scenario evidence. Do not map real relationships or pressure anyone to disclose personal information.
modules.assignment: Apply the Johari Window to two fictional characters in a teacher-provided scenario. Classify only scenario evidence as open, hidden, blind, or unknown; propose one respectful communication step that could expand the open area without pressuring disclosure. Submit: two labeled windows and a 300-word explanation. Include: at least two cited scenario details per character and one boundary-respecting communication step. Evaluation: correct classification (35%), evidence from the scenario (25%), ethical self-disclosure boundary (25%), and clarity (15%). Do not map real relationships or reveal private information.

modules.title: Small Group Communication
modules.objectives: Identify stages of group development and member roles; analyze factors that contribute to or detract from group effectiveness. Students will analyze model texts, draft or revise written responses, and support claims with textual evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: Communication in the Real World §13.2 — group development, socialization, cohesion, climate, roles, and Tuckman’s forming-through-adjourning model.
modules.videoNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.practiceNote: Use §13.3 to analyze decision quality, participation, groupthink risk, and constructive member roles in a teacher-provided fictional team case or a publicly documented example.
modules.assignment: Use a teacher-provided fictional team case, a public documented team example, or a de-identified hypothetical. Write a 400-word analysis applying Tuckman’s forming, storming, norming, performing, and adjourning stages; identify two constructive and two harmful communication behaviors with evidence. Submit: a stage timeline and analysis. Include: scenario evidence for each assigned stage, two constructive behaviors, two harmful behaviors, and one justified improvement. Evaluation: stage accuracy (30%), evidence (30%), behavior analysis (25%), and organization/citation (15%).

modules.title: Organizational Communication
modules.objectives: Explain formal and informal communication flows within organizations; evaluate the impact of organizational culture on communication. Students will analyze model texts, draft or revise written responses, and support claims with textual evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: Introduction to Communication — “What Is Organizational Communication?” explains organizations as communication systems shaped by formal and informal messages, structure, culture, and relationships.
modules.videoNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.practiceNote: Use the chapter’s systems lens to map formal and informal message flows for a teacher-provided fictional organization or a publicly documented organization. Do not use interviews, private messages, or confidential workplace information.
modules.assignment: Analyze a fictional organization chart and message set supplied in the module, or use publicly documented communications from an organization. Map formal downward, upward, and horizontal channels plus one informal channel; identify one bottleneck and recommend a repair. Submit: a communication-flow diagram and a 350-word report. Include: message sender/receiver, channel type, evidence for the bottleneck, and one justified repair. Evaluation: channel classification (30%), evidence (25%), bottleneck diagnosis (25%), recommendation and clarity (20%). No workplace interview, confidential information, or private messages are required.

quizQuestions.question: Which model treats communication as alternating sender and receiver turns with feedback, rather than simultaneous co-creation?
options: Linear model
Interactive model
Transactional model
Aristotle model
quizQuestions.answer: Interactive model
quizQuestions.explanation: The interactive model adds feedback but keeps participants in alternating sender and receiver roles; the transactional model treats both as simultaneous communicators.

quizQuestions.question: In the communication process, 'noise' refers to:
options: Only loud sounds that interrupt speech
Any interference that distorts the message
The tone of voice used by the sender
The medium through which a message travels
quizQuestions.answer: Any interference that distorts the message
quizQuestions.explanation: Noise is any physical, psychological, or semantic interference that distorts or disrupts the accurate transmission and reception of a message.

quizQuestions.question: Which part of a communication model includes the physical setting, relationship, and cultural expectations surrounding a message?
options: Feedback
Context
Channel
Encoding
quizQuestions.answer: Context
quizQuestions.explanation: Context includes the setting, relationship, history, and cultural expectations that shape how communicators encode and interpret a message.

quizQuestions.question: Short response: Complete this statement: The original linear model of communication was developed by...
quizQuestions.answer: The original linear model of communication is commonly identified as the Shannon-Weaver model, developed from Claude Shannon's work and popularized with Warren Weaver.
quizQuestions.explanation: This model treats communication as a message moving from sender to receiver through a channel, with noise possibly interfering along the way.

quizQuestions.question: The study of the relationship between language and meaning is called:
options: Syntax
Phonology
Semantics
Pragmatics
quizQuestions.answer: Semantics
quizQuestions.explanation: Semantics is the branch of linguistics concerned with meaning — how words and sentences carry and convey meaning.

quizQuestions.question: Which type of language refers to the emotional associations a word carries beyond its dictionary definition?
options: Denotative meaning
Connotative meaning
Abstract language
Equivocal language
quizQuestions.answer: Connotative meaning
quizQuestions.explanation: Connotative meaning includes the emotional, cultural, or personal associations attached to a word, beyond its literal denotative definition.

quizQuestions.question: Using vague or abstract words that can be interpreted in multiple ways is called using:
options: Euphemistic language
Equivocal language
Concrete language
Jargon
quizQuestions.answer: Equivocal language
quizQuestions.explanation: Equivocal language consists of words or phrases that have more than one commonly accepted meaning, which can cause misunderstanding.

quizQuestions.question: Which statement best distinguishes denotation from connotation?
options: Denotation is a word’s conventional dictionary meaning; connotation is the associated feeling or cultural meaning
Denotation is nonverbal; connotation is always spoken
Denotation changes by speaker; connotation never changes
Denotation is informal slang; connotation is formal grammar
quizQuestions.answer: Denotation is a word’s conventional dictionary meaning; connotation is the associated feeling or cultural meaning
quizQuestions.explanation: Denotation names the conventional referent, while connotation includes emotional and cultural associations.

quizQuestions.question: In Mehrabian’s studies of inconsistent messages about attitude or liking, which channels strongly influenced how the attitude was interpreted?
options: Words alone
Vocal tone and facial expression
Written follow-up only
Communication technology
quizQuestions.answer: Vocal tone and facial expression
quizQuestions.explanation: The finding applies to inconsistent attitude messages: listeners relied strongly on vocal and facial cues when those cues conflicted with the words.

quizQuestions.question: The study of personal space and how people use physical distance in communication is called:
options: Kinesics
Haptics
Proxemics
Chronemics
quizQuestions.answer: Proxemics
quizQuestions.explanation: Proxemics, developed by Edward Hall, is the study of how people perceive and use space in communication, including intimate, personal, social, and public zones.

quizQuestions.question: Which of the following is an example of paralanguage?
options: A gesture that replaces a spoken word
The rate, pitch, and volume of speech
The distance maintained between speakers
Eye contact patterns
quizQuestions.answer: The rate, pitch, and volume of speech
quizQuestions.explanation: Paralanguage refers to vocal elements that accompany spoken words, including rate, pitch, volume, and intonation, but not the words themselves.

quizQuestions.question: Short response: Define or explain: Nonverbal communication that manages the flow of conversation (e.g., nodding to indicate 'keep talking') is called.
quizQuestions.answer: Nonverbal communication that manages the flow of conversation is called a regulator, such as nodding, eye contact, or gestures that signal turn-taking.
quizQuestions.explanation: Regulators do not mainly express emotion or replace words; they coordinate when people start, continue, pause, or stop speaking.

quizQuestions.question: Which of the following best describes active listening?
options: Hearing the words spoken while multitasking
Fully concentrating on, understanding, and responding to a speaker
Waiting silently until the speaker finishes to plan your reply
Agreeing with everything the speaker says
quizQuestions.answer: Fully concentrating on, understanding, and responding to a speaker
quizQuestions.explanation: Active listening involves full attention, understanding, and engaged response to the speaker, going beyond mere hearing to genuine comprehension.

quizQuestions.question: Paraphrasing in active listening means:
options: Repeating the speaker's exact words back to them
Restating the speaker's message in your own words to confirm understanding
Asking a new question to change the topic
Summarizing only the emotional content of the message
quizQuestions.answer: Restating the speaker's message in your own words to confirm understanding
quizQuestions.explanation: Paraphrasing involves restating the speaker's message in your own words to confirm you understood correctly and show you were paying attention.

quizQuestions.question: Which listening barrier involves mentally preparing your response while the other person is still speaking?
options: Selective listening
Pseudo-listening
Rehearsal
Information overload
quizQuestions.answer: Rehearsal
quizQuestions.explanation: Rehearsal is the barrier where the listener is mentally composing a reply rather than fully attending to what the speaker is saying.

quizQuestions.question: Evaluative feedback in communication is best described as feedback that:
options: Describes behavior without judgment
Judges or assesses the worth of the message or the speaker
Asks for clarification about the message
Reflects the speaker's emotions back to them
quizQuestions.answer: Judges or assesses the worth of the message or the speaker
quizQuestions.explanation: Evaluative feedback makes a judgment about the message or person (e.g., 'That was a bad idea'), as opposed to descriptive or empathic feedback.

quizQuestions.question: Intrapersonal communication refers to:
options: Communication between two close friends
Communication that occurs within one's own mind
Communication in large public settings
Communication through mass media
quizQuestions.answer: Communication that occurs within one's own mind
quizQuestions.explanation: Intrapersonal communication is the internal dialogue and self-talk that occurs within an individual's own mind.

quizQuestions.question: Self-concept is best defined as:
options: How others perceive you
Your overall subjective evaluation of your own worth
The mental image you hold of yourself
Your awareness of others' feelings
quizQuestions.answer: The mental image you hold of yourself
quizQuestions.explanation: Self-concept is the mental image or perception an individual holds of themselves, encompassing beliefs about one's personality, abilities, and roles.

quizQuestions.question: How can intrapersonal communication affect an interaction with someone else?
options: Internal expectations can shape attention, interpretation, and the response a person chooses
Self-talk has no effect once another person is present
It determines the other person’s intent with certainty
It replaces the need to listen for feedback
quizQuestions.answer: Internal expectations can shape attention, interpretation, and the response a person chooses
quizQuestions.explanation: Internal messages can prime how someone notices cues and responds, but they do not prove another person’s intent.

quizQuestions.question: What is reflected appraisal?
options: Building a self-concept partly from how we believe significant others perceive us
Judging another person only from their appearance
Repeating a message until it is accepted
Separating verbal messages from nonverbal cues
quizQuestions.answer: Building a self-concept partly from how we believe significant others perceive us
quizQuestions.explanation: Reflected appraisal describes how perceived feedback from others contributes to self-concept.

quizQuestions.question: The Johari Window model helps individuals understand:
options: How messages are encoded and decoded
The relationship between self-disclosure and mutual awareness
The stages of group development
How conflict escalates in organizations
quizQuestions.answer: The relationship between self-disclosure and mutual awareness
quizQuestions.explanation: The Johari Window is a tool for understanding self-disclosure and interpersonal awareness, depicting information known/unknown to self and others in four quadrants.

quizQuestions.question: Self-disclosure in interpersonal communication refers to:
options: Revealing information about yourself to others
Listening carefully to what another person says
Keeping personal information private in professional settings
Offering feedback on another person's behavior
quizQuestions.answer: Revealing information about yourself to others
quizQuestions.explanation: Self-disclosure is the intentional act of sharing personal information — thoughts, feelings, or experiences — with another person.

quizQuestions.question: Social Penetration Theory, developed by Altman and Taylor, describes relationships as progressing through:
options: Five fixed stages that always occur in order
Increasing breadth and depth of self-disclosure over time
Cycles of conflict and resolution
Networks of overlapping social roles
quizQuestions.answer: Increasing breadth and depth of self-disclosure over time
quizQuestions.explanation: Social Penetration Theory uses an 'onion' metaphor, proposing that relationships develop as self-disclosure increases in both breadth (topics) and depth (intimacy).

quizQuestions.question: Which self-disclosure choice is most appropriate?
options: Share increasingly private details as quickly as possible
Choose relevant information, consider trust and context, and respect both people’s boundaries
Avoid all feedback after disclosing
Require the other person to disclose the same amount immediately
quizQuestions.answer: Choose relevant information, consider trust and context, and respect both people’s boundaries
quizQuestions.explanation: Appropriate self-disclosure is purposeful, gradual, context-sensitive, and voluntary. Trust does not create an obligation to reveal private information or to match another person’s disclosure immediately.

quizQuestions.question: Describe the stable-exchange stage of social penetration theory.
quizQuestions.answer: At the stable-exchange stage, people communicate with deep openness, high trust, and enough shared understanding to predict each other’s reactions.
quizQuestions.explanation: Stable exchange is the mature stage of social penetration, marked by breadth, depth, spontaneity, and mutual understanding.

quizQuestions.question: According to Tuckman's model, in which stage do group members first experience conflict and power struggles?
options: Forming
Storming
Norming
Performing
quizQuestions.answer: Storming
quizQuestions.explanation: In the Storming stage, group members begin to assert ideas and compete for positions, leading to interpersonal conflict and tension before norms are established.

quizQuestions.question: A 'task role' in small group communication is best described as a role that:
options: Maintains emotional harmony within the group
Helps the group achieve its goals and complete work
Promotes individual interests over group goals
Provides social support to discouraged members
quizQuestions.answer: Helps the group achieve its goals and complete work
quizQuestions.explanation: Task roles (e.g., initiator, information seeker, clarifier) are behaviors that help the group accomplish its assigned work and reach its objectives.

quizQuestions.question: Which practice most directly reduces groupthink?
options: A leader states a preferred answer before discussion
The group discourages dissent to preserve harmony
The group assigns a devil’s advocate and invites independent alternatives before deciding
Members vote before reviewing evidence
quizQuestions.answer: The group assigns a devil’s advocate and invites independent alternatives before deciding
quizQuestions.explanation: Structured dissent and independent alternatives make it harder for pressure toward consensus to suppress relevant evidence.

quizQuestions.question: Short response: Complete this statement: In tuckman's model, the norming stage is characterized by...
quizQuestions.answer: In Tuckman's model, the norming stage is characterized by clearer roles, shared expectations, stronger cohesion, and more cooperative group behavior.
quizQuestions.explanation: After the conflict of storming, groups in the norming stage establish norms and begin functioning with more trust and coordination.

quizQuestions.question: Downward communication in an organization flows:
options: From employees to management
From managers to subordinates
Between departments at the same level
From the organization to external stakeholders
quizQuestions.answer: From managers to subordinates
quizQuestions.explanation: Downward communication flows from higher levels of the organizational hierarchy (managers) to lower levels (subordinates), conveying instructions and policies.

quizQuestions.question: The 'grapevine' in organizational communication refers to:
options: Official memos circulated through management channels
Informal information networks among employees
A visual chart of the organization's structure
A formal process for filing employee grievances
quizQuestions.answer: Informal information networks among employees
quizQuestions.explanation: The organizational grapevine is the informal, unofficial network of communication among employees that travels outside of formal channels.

quizQuestions.question: Horizontal communication in an organization refers to communication:
options: From executives to all employees
Between people at the same hierarchical level
From employees to top management
Between the organization and the public
quizQuestions.answer: Between people at the same hierarchical level
quizQuestions.explanation: Horizontal (or lateral) communication occurs between employees, departments, or teams at the same level of the organizational hierarchy.

quizQuestions.question: Which example is horizontal communication?
options: A supervisor assigns a task to an employee
An employee submits a concern to a director
Two department managers at the same organizational level coordinate a shared deadline
A company publishes an advertisement to customers
quizQuestions.answer: Two department managers at the same organizational level coordinate a shared deadline
quizQuestions.explanation: Horizontal communication moves among people or units at similar levels of the hierarchy.

questions.question: Which communication model is most realistic because it shows both parties simultaneously sending and receiving messages?
options: Linear model
Interactive model
Transactional model
Aristotle's model
questions.answer: Transactional model
questions.explanation: The transactional model reflects the simultaneous, mutually influential nature of real communication, where all parties act as senders and receivers at the same time.

questions.question: Semantic noise is best described as:
options: Loud environmental sounds that interrupt speech
Differences in word meaning that cause misunderstanding
Technical problems with communication technology
Physical distractions in the communication environment
questions.answer: Differences in word meaning that cause misunderstanding
questions.explanation: Semantic noise occurs when words or symbols mean different things to the sender and receiver, causing the message to be misinterpreted.

questions.question: The difference between denotative and connotative meaning is that:
options: Denotative meaning is emotional; connotative meaning is literal
Denotative meaning is the dictionary definition; connotative meaning includes emotional associations
Connotative meaning is precise; denotative meaning is vague
They refer to the same concept from different communication traditions
questions.answer: Denotative meaning is the dictionary definition; connotative meaning includes emotional associations
questions.explanation: Denotative meaning is the objective, dictionary definition of a word; connotative meaning includes the subjective, emotional, and cultural associations the word carries.

questions.question: A student compares how close people stand during conversations in different settings. Which area of nonverbal communication is the student examining?
options: How people use space and physical distance in communication
How vocal pitch and volume shape meaning
How time communicates status and urgency
How touch functions in relationships
questions.answer: How people use space and physical distance in communication
questions.explanation: Proxemics examines the communicative use of space, distance, and territoriality. The scenario focuses on interpersonal distance rather than voice, time, or touch.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of active listening?
options: Maintaining eye contact with the speaker
Paraphrasing to confirm understanding
Internally planning your response while the speaker talks
Using minimal encouragers like nodding
questions.answer: Internally planning your response while the speaker talks
questions.explanation: Planning your response while someone is talking (rehearsal) is a barrier to active listening, not a characteristic of it; active listeners focus fully on the speaker.

questions.question: The 'looking-glass self' theory suggests that self-concept develops through:
options: Comparison with idealized images in media
Imagining how others perceive and evaluate us
Biological and genetic predispositions
Childhood experiences with parents and authority figures
questions.answer: Imagining how others perceive and evaluate us
questions.explanation: Charles Cooley's looking-glass self theory proposes that individuals form self-concept based on how they imagine they appear to others and how they imagine others judge them.

questions.question: The Johari Window quadrant labeled 'Hidden Area' contains information that:
questions.answer: The Hidden Area contains information known to the self but not shared with others, such as private feelings, experiences, or concerns.
questions.explanation: In the Johari Window, hidden information can become part of the open area through appropriate self-disclosure.

questions.question: What does the onion metaphor in social penetration theory represent?
options: Relationships deepen through gradual disclosure across breadth and depth
Conflict automatically strengthens every relationship
Only nonverbal behavior creates intimacy
Trust develops in one irreversible step
questions.answer: Relationships deepen through gradual disclosure across breadth and depth
questions.explanation: The metaphor represents layers of information becoming accessible over time through reciprocal, appropriate disclosure.

questions.question: In which stage of Tuckman's group development model does the group reach its highest level of productivity?
options: Forming
Storming
Norming
Performing
questions.answer: Performing
questions.explanation: The Performing stage is when the group has resolved interpersonal issues, established roles, and is functioning at peak effectiveness toward its goals.

questions.question: Groupthink is most likely to occur in groups that are:
options: Large, diverse, and newly formed
Highly cohesive and under pressure to reach quick consensus
Made up of members with low investment in outcomes
Led by a leader who actively encourages dissent
questions.answer: Highly cohesive and under pressure to reach quick consensus
questions.explanation: Groupthink is most common in highly cohesive groups facing pressure, where maintaining harmony becomes more important than evaluating alternatives critically.

questions.question: Which behavior is an example of a task role in a small group?
options: Summarizing the team’s evidence and next decision
Telling jokes to reduce tension
Encouraging a quiet member without discussing the task
Expressing personal approval of every idea
questions.answer: Summarizing the team’s evidence and next decision
questions.explanation: Task roles move the group’s work forward by organizing information, clarifying decisions, and coordinating the next action.

questions.question: Why are clear group norms useful?
options: They eliminate every disagreement
They establish shared expectations for participation, evidence, deadlines, and conflict
They guarantee that the leader is always correct
They replace the need for feedback
questions.answer: They establish shared expectations for participation, evidence, deadlines, and conflict
questions.explanation: Clear norms make expectations visible, help members coordinate work, and create a fair basis for addressing missed commitments or harmful behavior.

questions.question: Which listener response best demonstrates active listening?
options: Plan a rebuttal while the speaker continues
Paraphrase the speaker’s point and ask whether the paraphrase is accurate
Change the topic to a similar personal experience
Offer advice before checking what the speaker means
questions.answer: Paraphrase the speaker’s point and ask whether the paraphrase is accurate
questions.explanation: Paraphrasing and checking accuracy provide feedback, test understanding, and keep attention on the speaker’s intended meaning.

questions.question: In the Johari Window, the Blind Area contains information that is:
options: Known to self and known to others
Known to self but not known to others
Not known to self but noticed by others
Unknown to both self and others
questions.answer: Not known to self but noticed by others
questions.explanation: The Blind Area represents behaviors or effects that other people notice but the person has not yet recognized about themself.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of an emblem in nonverbal communication?
options: Scratching your nose when nervous
Using hand gestures to emphasize a spoken point
Giving a thumbs-up to mean 'OK' or 'good'
Adjusting your posture when the topic becomes serious
questions.answer: Giving a thumbs-up to mean 'OK' or 'good'
questions.explanation: Emblems are gestures with specific, culturally shared verbal translations that can stand alone without spoken words, such as the thumbs-up for approval.

questions.question: What was the Shannon-Weaver model originally designed to represent?
options: Technical transmission of a signal from sender through a channel to receiver
Simultaneous face-to-face meaning-making
Stages of small-group development
Cultural differences in workplace communication
questions.answer: Technical transmission of a signal from sender through a channel to receiver
questions.explanation: The model began as a mathematical account of signal transmission and noise, then influenced later human-communication models.

questions.question: Abstract language is problematic in communication because it:
options: Is too technical for most audiences to understand
Lacks specificity and can be interpreted in multiple ways
Carries strong negative connotations for listeners
Relies too heavily on nonverbal cues for meaning
questions.answer: Lacks specificity and can be interpreted in multiple ways
questions.explanation: Abstract language (e.g., 'improve performance' vs. 'submit reports by 5 PM') lacks the specific referents needed for a shared, unambiguous meaning.

questions.question: In Communication Studies final concepts, Kinesics is the study of:
options: The use of physical space in communication
Body movement and gesture as communication
The meaning of touch in social interaction
Time as a communicative resource
questions.answer: Body movement and gesture as communication
questions.explanation: Kinesics is the study of body language — gestures, facial expressions, eye contact, and posture — as forms of nonverbal communication.

questions.question: Which listening style involves focusing exclusively on facts and data while filtering out emotional content?
options: Empathic listening
Appreciative listening
Comprehensive listening
Analytical listening
questions.answer: Analytical listening
questions.explanation: Analytical (or critical) listening focuses on evaluating and analyzing the informational content of a message, often setting aside emotional dimensions.

questions.question: Which feature most clearly distinguishes the transactional model of communication?
options: A message moves one way from sender to receiver
Participants simultaneously send, receive, and adapt messages within a shared context
Feedback occurs only after the conversation ends
Noise is excluded from the model
questions.answer: Participants simultaneously send, receive, and adapt messages within a shared context
questions.explanation: The transactional model treats meaning as jointly created while both communicators continuously send, receive, and adapt cues.

questions.question: Which statement best explains connotative meaning?
options: The dictionary definition shared by a speech community
The emotional and cultural associations a word carries beyond its literal definition
A message sent without a channel
A gesture that replaces a spoken word
questions.answer: The emotional and cultural associations a word carries beyond its literal definition
questions.explanation: Connotation consists of learned emotional and cultural associations, so different audiences may react differently to the same word.

questions.question: A student understands every word in a lecture but cannot focus because of anxiety about an exam. What kind of noise is this?
options: Physical noise
Psychological noise
Semantic noise
Channel feedback
questions.answer: Psychological noise
questions.explanation: Anxiety is an internal mental distraction, so it is psychological noise even when the words and physical channel are clear.

questions.question: A researcher studies how seating distance changes participation in a meeting. Which nonverbal category is central?
options: Kinesics
Proxemics
Chronemics
Haptics
questions.answer: Proxemics
questions.explanation: Proxemics examines how communicators use physical space and distance, including seating arrangements and interpersonal distance.

questions.question: Which response is the best paraphrase check during active listening?
options: You should just do what I did.
So you need a later deadline because the data arrived late; did I understand correctly?
That is not a serious problem.
Let me tell you a different story.
questions.answer: So you need a later deadline because the data arrived late; did I understand correctly?
questions.explanation: The response restates both the need and reason, then invites correction instead of judging, advising, or shifting attention.

questions.question: Why can constructive self-talk change outward communication?
options: It guarantees that other people will agree
Internal messages can shape perception, emotion, and the choices a communicator makes
It removes the need for feedback
It converts every hidden thought into public information
questions.answer: Internal messages can shape perception, emotion, and the choices a communicator makes
questions.explanation: Intrapersonal communication influences how a person interprets a situation and selects tone, wording, and behavior in later interaction.

questions.question: Which action can ethically reduce a Johari Window Blind Area?
options: Demand private disclosure
Ask for specific, respectful feedback about an observable behavior
Guess another person’s hidden motives
Share confidential information publicly
questions.answer: Ask for specific, respectful feedback about an observable behavior
questions.explanation: Specific feedback can reveal an effect the person has not noticed while keeping the exchange bounded to observable behavior.

questions.question: In social penetration theory, what do breadth and depth describe?
options: The number of channels and speed of feedback
The range of topics disclosed and how personal the disclosure becomes
Group size and meeting length
Formal and informal organizational networks
questions.answer: The range of topics disclosed and how personal the disclosure becomes
questions.explanation: Breadth is the range of subjects shared, while depth is the degree of personal or intimate information disclosed over time.

questions.question: Which condition most increases the risk of groupthink?
options: The leader invites independent objections before stating a preference
Members feel pressure to preserve unanimity and suppress doubts
The group assigns a devil’s advocate
The team compares multiple alternatives
questions.answer: Members feel pressure to preserve unanimity and suppress doubts
questions.explanation: Groupthink grows when cohesion and consensus pressure discourage members from raising contrary evidence or evaluating alternatives.

questions.question: What usually characterizes Tuckman’s storming stage?
options: Members orient to the task and seek initial acceptance
Conflict emerges over roles, goals, or methods as members assert different views
Norms are stable and performance is consistently high
The group closes the task and reflects on its work
questions.answer: Conflict emerges over roles, goals, or methods as members assert different views
questions.explanation: Storming involves disagreement and role negotiation; resolving it constructively helps the group establish workable norms.

questions.question: Which message is an example of upward organizational communication?
options: A supervisor assigns tasks to employees
An employee reports a safety concern to a manager
Two department peers coordinate a shared deadline
A company sends an advertisement to customers
questions.answer: An employee reports a safety concern to a manager
questions.explanation: Upward communication moves from a lower organizational level to a higher one, such as an employee reporting evidence or concerns.

questions.question: What is the organizational grapevine?
options: A formal policy archive
An informal peer-to-peer communication network
A required annual report
A downward chain of command
questions.answer: An informal peer-to-peer communication network
questions.explanation: The grapevine carries unofficial information through relationships rather than through the organization’s formal reporting structure.

questions.question: Which Tuckman stage addresses closure after a group completes its task?
options: Forming
Storming
Performing
Adjourning
questions.answer: Adjourning
questions.explanation: Adjourning includes closure, evaluation, transition, and disbanding after the group’s work ends.

questions.question: Which group behavior is most constructive when evidence conflicts with the team’s preferred plan?
options: Hide the evidence to protect morale
Name the concern, show the evidence, and invite the team to test the plan
Wait until after implementation to mention it
Attack the person who proposed the plan
questions.answer: Name the concern, show the evidence, and invite the team to test the plan
questions.explanation: Constructive group communication surfaces a claim and evidence while inviting joint evaluation instead of silence or personal attack.

questions.question: Which leadership move best reduces groupthink?
options: State the preferred answer before discussion
Reward quick agreement
Ask members to develop independent alternatives and assign a devil’s advocate
Exclude dissenting members
questions.answer: Ask members to develop independent alternatives and assign a devil’s advocate
questions.explanation: Independent alternatives and a designated challenge role make dissent legitimate and improve the group’s evaluation of evidence.

questions.question: A department repeatedly misses urgent messages because updates pass through one overloaded manager. What is the best first repair?
options: Add more informal rumors
Map the bottleneck and create a documented backup or horizontal channel
Stop all upward communication
Send every message to the entire organization
questions.answer: Map the bottleneck and create a documented backup or horizontal channel
questions.explanation: The repair addresses the identified flow bottleneck while preserving accountability and giving urgent information a reliable alternate path.
